transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Thank you so much for fitting me in, I really appreciate it. Um, well, I hope I'm not wasting your time, it's probably nothing major, but... my family and some of my colleagues suggested I talk to someone. 

It's just that I have this habit where I keep getting up when everyone else is seated. Like, during our staff meetings at the school—I'm a teacher—or even just sitting around the dinner table at home. I'll suddenly just get up because I feel like I need to refill the coffee, or go double-check a handout, or I'll just walk to the back of the room. And nothing is really urgent, you know? I just sort of... do it. I always try to frame it as being helpful, so it's not like I'm trying to be disruptive or rude! I just have a hard time staying in my chair. 

I hope I'm explaining that right. Is that the kind of information you're looking for?
Can you tell me when you first started noticing this restlessness and difficulty staying seated—did it begin in childhood, or is this something that started more recently in adulthood?

Oh, well... I suppose it's actually been going on for a very long time. Really, since I was a little girl. 

I mean, I was a good student! My report cards always said I was bright, which my parents were very proud of. But, um... the teachers would also usually write that I couldn't quite stay in my seat, or that I had a hard time waiting my turn. I think I just got so eager to participate, you know? I certainly wasn't trying to be a troublemaker or anything like that. 

My mother, bless her, she actually used to joke that I wore a path right into the classroom floor between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten years old. I just always needed a little excuse to be up and moving around. 

So, yes, it definitely started back in childhood. Is that... is that the kind of background you need? I hope I'm giving you the right information.
Besides the restlessness, do you also notice problems like having trouble staying focused on tasks, frequently losing track of things, or getting easily distracted, both now and back in school?

Oh, um... no, not really. I hope it doesn't sound like I'm being difficult, but I actually pride myself on being quite organized! I mean, as a teacher, you sort of have to be, right? 

I keep very careful track of my lesson plans and my grading, and I always know where my keys are. I don't really lose track of what I'm doing. And even back in school, I could always focus on the actual work... I just, well, I liked to focus on it while standing at the back of the room, if that makes sense. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I get distracted easily or lose focus. It's really just the... the needing to move around part. Is that alright? I hope that's a helpful answer for you, I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture of how things are.
Do you often find yourself interrupting conversations, blurting out answers before a question is finished, or having trouble waiting your turn in lines or discussions?

Oh dear, well... I suppose I do do that a little bit. But I promise it's never meant to be rude! I just get so... enthusiastic, I think. 

Like, when we're having group discussions—especially at my book club, or during our curriculum meetings at school—I'll often just sort of jump in before someone has completely finished their thought. It's just that the response is already right there in my head, and I end up blurting it out before I can really stop myself. I always try to apologize right away and let them finish, of course! I just get so swept up in the conversation and excited about the topic. 

Does that make sense? I hope that doesn't make me sound like a terrible listener or a bad colleague. I really do try my best to be polite. Is that the sort of thing you were asking about?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a longstanding, childhood-onset pattern of motor restlessness (difficulty remaining seated, needing to get up and move during meetings, classroom, meals), impulsivity (interrupting conversations, blurting out responses, difficulty waiting turn), present across multiple settings (school, home, work, book club). She explicitly denies significant inattentive symptoms (no difficulty sustaining focus, no losing track of things, good organizational skills), ruling out combined or inattentive presentations. Symptoms began before age 12, have persisted into adulthood, and cause functional friction in professional and social settings, though she minimizes impairment. This pattern is most consistent with ADHD, Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Presentation (F90.1) rather than Combined Type (F90.2) or Predominantly Inattentive Type (F90.0).
